newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-GSM phones seen ringing up 100 million users.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-GSM phones seen ringing up 100 million users.

text.p: The market for GSM digital mobile telephones is set for a surge in growth but competition between operators and equipment manufacturers is going to be merciless, industry sources say.

"At the end of 1998 we will be looking at a figure of 100 million GSM subscribers," Nigel Cawthorne, managing research editor of the World Cellular Database, said in an opening speech at the GSM World Congress on Wednesday.
This compares with 33 million at the end of 1996 and 13 million at the end of 1995, he said.
GSM, Global System for Mobile telecommunications, began as a European grouping trying to get common standards in many countries for digital mobile communications.
The United States and Japan have developed their own versions but GSM is winning market share there as well, Cawthorne said.
Technically there are still many differences between various versions of the digital mobile phone, especially in the frequencies used for the radio link by the GSM, DCS-1800 and PCS-1900 systems.
But according to officials at Motorola Inc, these differences will soon melt away as new chipsets allow mobile phones to interact with any frequency.

Gretel Hoffman, outgoing chairperson of the GSM association, said that during 1997 the industry had to develop and produce "tri-band" equipment so that the customer could use a phone irrespective of the system used by the operator.
DCS-1800, which uses a frequency twice the rate of a "normal" GSM, has seen particularly fast growth recently.
Bouygues Telecom uses the system in France, Mercury One-2-One and Orange in Britain and E-plus in Germany.
Telecom equipment makers said their first priority would be to get "dual-band" equipment for GSM and DCS-1800, before adding the PCS-1900 system of the United States.

Standard hand sets for all three systems would reduce production costs, a key factor in a very competitive market which saw prices fall by 10 to 15 percent in 1996 and could see a bigger drop in 1997, producers said.
Operators are subsidising the hand sets heavily, sometimes giving them away or selling them at less than a third of real costs in order to lure customers to sign up for subscriptions.

The key to growth will remain professional users but mobile telecommunications is starting to turn into a mass market and further phone price reductions and cuts in call rates are expected to boost this trend, industry sources say.
In their search for market share, companies are looking at additional services to go along with the phone, such as Internet access, easy connections with laptop computers or special dialling codes.
"1997 is going to be the year of value added services," said Alain Bravo, president of the mobile communications division of Alcatel Alsthom.

Sweden's LM Ericsson AB, Motorola and Alcatel are all developing services that will link mobile phones to a company's internal telecommunications system -- allowing a user to dial extension numbers or short dialling codes as if he or she were using a telephone in the office.
Another approach is to link mobile phones to third parties with a "loyalty factor". This would connect them to a bank, retailer, airline or car rental company -- or a combination.
Already operators are experimenting with offering weather information, restaurant booking, travel updates and other services on top of the basic portable telephone.
And there is a move towards miniaturisation with Ericsson unveiling the smallest phone and Alcatel launching the flattest phone -- all aimed at making the portable less conspicuous.
The GSM World Congress, which will last for three days in this Mediterranean resort, is being attended by more than 850 operators from around 72 countries.
